title: He Lost ₹47 Lakh Following "Expert" Advice
summary: Here's What He Wishes He Knew 7 Years Ago
author: BM Wealth Editorial Team
content: By BM Wealth Editorial Team
December 9, 2025 | 8-Minute Read | Investment Education
True story from Mumbai. Names and details changed for privacy.
The message arrived at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday:
"Sir, please... can you check my father's investments? Something feels very wrong."

The voice on the call was shaking. A 29-year-old software engineer from Borivali, calling about his father—a successful chartered accountant who lives in a comfortable 2BHK in Bandra, drives a Honda City, and has been investing diligently for 18 years.
The next morning, we connected on video call. He shared his screen.
A folder opened. Inside were dozens of documents:
→	Five mutual fund statements (all different fund houses, no clear strategy)
→	Three ULIP policies with 5-year lock-in periods
→	Two traditional insurance plans marketed as "investment schemes"
→	Multiple "guaranteed return" endowment plans
→	Several debt funds with expense ratios above 2%
Everything scattered. Nothing aligned. No clear financial goals documented anywhere.
The Number That Changed Everything
We spent three hours analyzing the portfolio. Running calculations. Comparing historical market data. Checking expense ratios. Understanding the actual product structures.
Then came the moment that made the room go quiet.
We compared:
What his portfolio actually delivered over 7 years
versus
What a simple, goal-aligned, properly structured portfolio could have delivered historically in the same period (based on market data from similar time frames).
The opportunity cost: ₹47,00,000
Not ₹47,000. Not ₹4.7 lakh. Nearly half a crore rupees in potential wealth—gone.
How Does This Even Happen?
Here's what most people don't understand: This wasn't a case of fraud. The father wasn't scammed. He wasn't cheated.
He was simply sold products that didn't match his actual financial goals.
The core problems we identified:
1. Product Selection Without Goal Mapping

He was buying "investment products" without first defining what he was actually investing FOR. Retirement? Child's education? Emergency fund? Wealth creation? Each goal needs a different strategy, timeline, and risk approach. He had products, but no plan.
2. Mixing Insurance with Investment

Three ULIPs and two traditional endowment plans. These products combine life insurance with investment—and historically, they do neither particularly well. High charges eat into returns. Lock-in periods trap capital. The insurance coverage is usually inadequate for actual family needs.
3. High-Cost Products Eating Returns Silently

Some of his mutual funds had expense ratios above 2%. Over 15-20 years, these charges compound into massive wealth destruction. A 2% annual charge on ₹10 lakh growing at 12% for 20 years can cost you over ₹12 lakh in lost returns. Most investors never even check this number.
4. No Asset Allocation Strategy

His portfolio had no clear equity-debt split aligned to his age, risk capacity, or financial goals. Some years he was 90% equity (too risky for his situation). Other years, 70% debt (too conservative for wealth building). Asset allocation—not product selection—determines 80-90% of portfolio returns over time.
5. Zero Portfolio Review for 7 Years

Once products were sold, there was no systematic annual review. No rebalancing. No checking if funds were underperforming. No adjusting strategy as life situations changed. The portfolio was on autopilot—with no pilot actually monitoring the flight.
When we finished explaining these issues, the son was silent for a full minute.
"My father trusted someone completely. He did everything they told him to do. And this is the result."
This is the painful reality for millions of Indian families. Sincerity without proper financial guidance can be extremely expensive.
The Part That Hurts Most
This wasn't a careless investor. This was a CA—someone who understands numbers, analyzes balance sheets for clients, and makes careful financial decisions professionally.
He worked 10-12 hour days. Saved diligently. Invested regularly. Did everything right from a discipline perspective.
The only thing he didn't do? Ask the right questions about product suitability, cost structure, and goal alignment before committing his hard-earned money.
If someone this financially aware can lose ₹47 lakh in opportunity cost, imagine what's happening to families without this background.
What Every Investor Must Understand
After reviewing 200+ portfolios over the past decade, certain patterns emerge clearly. Here's what separates successful wealth builders from those who struggle:
→	Goals First, Products Second
Define clear financial goals with timelines BEFORE choosing any investment product. Retirement in 20 years needs different products than child's education in 8 years or buying a home in 3 years.
→	Keep Insurance and Investment Separate
Pure term insurance for life protection. Mutual funds/other vehicles for wealth creation. Mixing them typically serves neither purpose well.
→	Understand All Costs
Expense ratios, allocation charges, exit loads, lock-in periods—know exactly what you're paying and why. A 1% difference in annual costs can mean lakhs over decades.
→	Build Proper Asset Allocation
Your equity-debt-liquid mix should match your age, risk capacity, and time horizons for different goals. This drives 80-90% of long-term returns.
→	Review and Rebalance Annually
Markets move. Your situation changes. Funds underperform. Regular review ensures your portfolio stays aligned with goals, and rebalancing locks in gains while managing risk.
These aren't complicated strategies. They're fundamental principles. But they require someone to actually explain them clearly—which often doesn't happen.
Are You in the Same Situation?
Take 5 minutes right now. Pull out your investment statements. Check:
→	Can you explain WHY you own each specific investment?
→	Do you have any ULIPs or traditional insurance policies someone called "investment plans"?
→	Do you know the exact expense ratio of each mutual fund?
→	Is there a clear asset allocation strategy aligned to your goals?
→	When was the last time someone actually reviewed your portfolio comprehensively?
If you answered "I'm not sure" or "I don't know" to even one of these questions, there may be gaps that could cost you significantly over time.
What Changed for This Family

After our initial consultation, we spent time helping the family understand their actual financial situation—not with jargon, but with clear explanations of what they owned and why it might not be optimal.
We provided educational guidance on:
→	How to think about different financial goals systematically
→	General principles of asset allocation for different life stages
→	Understanding product costs and their long-term impact
→	The importance of separating insurance protection from investment growth
→	How regular portfolio review helps maintain alignment with changing life situations

18 months later, they have clarity. They understand where their money is, why it's there, and what it's meant to achieve. More importantly, they have a systematic approach to making future financial decisions.
That's the difference proper financial guidance makes—not selling products, but building understanding and strategy.

title: Building Wealth 101: A Mumbai Software Engineer's Journey from ₹0 to ₹25 Lakh
summary: How a 26-year-old in Andheri built real wealth in 4 years with just ₹10,000/month.
author: BM Wealth Editorial Team
content: By BM Wealth Editorial Team
January 10, 2025 | 7-Minute Read | Investment Education
The WhatsApp message was simple:
"Sir, my portfolio just crossed ₹25 lakh. Four years ago, I had ₹0 saved. Thank you for teaching me the basics."

Priya (name changed), a 26-year-old software engineer working in Andheri, didn't come from a wealthy family. She grew up in a modest 1BHK in Dahisar, took the Western Line local to work every day, and earned ₹6.5 lakh per year when she started her first job.
Today, she has ₹25.4 lakh invested across mutual funds, emergency savings, and PPF—built entirely from disciplined monthly contributions of ₹10,000 to ₹15,000.
Here's exactly what she did. No complicated strategies. No market timing. Just fundamental wealth-building principles applied consistently.
Step 1: Build Your Emergency Fund First (₹3-6 Months Expenses)
Before Priya invested a single rupee in equity, she built an emergency fund.
Living in Mumbai, her monthly expenses were roughly ₹25,000 (rent ₹12,000 for a shared 2BHK in Goregaon, food ₹6,000, local pass ₹400, utilities and miscellaneous ₹6,600).
She saved ₹75,000 (3 months expenses) in a liquid fund and high-interest savings account. This took her 8 months of saving ₹10,000/month from her salary.
Why this matters: When markets fell 15% in March 2020, she didn't need to sell her equity investments at a loss. Her emergency fund protected her long-term wealth-building plan.
Without this safety net, most investors panic-sell during market corrections—destroying years of compounding in a moment of fear.
Step 2: Automate Your Monthly Investments (Set and Forget)
Once her emergency fund was ready, Priya set up automatic SIPs:
→ ₹5,000/month in a Nifty 50 index fund
→ ₹3,000/month in a Nifty Next 50 index fund
→ ₹2,000/month in PPF (for tax benefit under 80C)
Total: ₹10,000/month automated on the 5th of every month (right after salary credit).
She never checked daily NAVs. Never tried to time the market. Never paused SIPs during corrections.
In 4 years, she invested ₹4.8 lakh through SIPs. That ₹4.8 lakh grew to ₹6.8 lakh in equity (approx. 15% CAGR including dividends reinvested). Her PPF accumulated ₹1.1 lakh (with interest).
Step 3: Keep Costs Low (Expense Ratios Below 0.5%)
Priya avoided actively managed funds with 2%+ expense ratios. She stuck to low-cost index funds charging 0.1-0.3% annually.
Over 20 years, a 1.5% difference in annual costs on ₹10 lakh can result in a loss of over ₹8 lakh in returns. She avoided this trap from day one.
Step 4: Increase SIPs Annually (₹10k → ₹15k → ₹20k)
Every year when she got a salary hike, Priya increased her SIP by 20-30%:
→ Year 1: ₹10,000/month
→ Year 2: ₹12,000/month
→ Year 3: ₹15,000/month
→ Year 4: ₹18,000/month
This single habit accelerated her wealth building dramatically. By Year 4, she was investing almost double her initial amount without feeling any lifestyle pinch.
Step 5: Review Twice a Year, Not Daily
Priya checked her portfolio only twice a year—in June and December.
She reviewed:
✓ Whether her asset allocation (equity-debt-liquid split) was still aligned with her 10-year goal
✓ If any fund was consistently underperforming its benchmark
✓ Whether she needed to rebalance (sell some equity, add to debt, or vice versa)
She never checked stock market news daily. Never panicked during corrections. Never tried to predict crashes.
This emotional discipline saved her from the biggest wealth destroyer: behavioral mistakes.
The Results After 4 Years
Priya's portfolio today:
→ Equity mutual funds: ₹18.2 lakh (₹13.8 lakh invested + ₹4.4 lakh gains)
→ PPF: ₹1.1 lakh
→ Emergency fund (liquid): ₹1.2 lakh
→ Additional savings in debt funds: ₹4.9 lakh
Total: ₹25.4 lakh
She started with ₹0. She never earned a massive salary. She didn't get lucky with crypto or stock tips. She just followed basic wealth-building principles with discipline.
What Makes This Work for Mumbai Professionals
If you're a young professional in Mumbai earning ₹5-10 lakh per year, here's what you need to do:
→ Start with Emergency Fund: Save 3-6 months expenses in liquid savings before investing in equity
→ Automate SIPs: Set up monthly investments right after salary credit
→ Keep Costs Low: Use index funds or low-cost actively managed funds (expense ratio under 1%)
→ Increase SIPs with Salary Hikes: Invest at least 30-40% of every increment
→ Review Twice a Year: Check asset allocation and rebalance; don't track daily NAVs
These aren't secrets. They're fundamentals. But they work only if you actually implement them consistently.
Your Action Plan (Start This Week)
Take 30 minutes this weekend. Do this:
1. Calculate your monthly expenses. Multiply by 3 or 6. That's your emergency fund target.
2. Open a liquid fund or high-interest savings account. Start saving for this first.
3. Once emergency fund is ready, open a mutual fund account (any major platform).
4. Set up automated SIPs in 1-2 index funds (Nifty 50, Nifty Next 50).
5. Set calendar reminders for June and December to review your portfolio.
That's it. No complexity. No jargon. Just basics executed consistently.
Four years from now, you'll have built real wealth—just like Priya.

title: Risk Management Playbook: How a Powai Family Protected ₹80 Lakh During Market Crashes
summary: The asset allocation strategy that saved this family's retirement when Nifty fell 25%.
author: BM Wealth Editorial Team
content: By BM Wealth Editorial Team
January 24, 2025 | 9-Minute Read | Investment Education
March 2020. Markets crashed 25% in 3 weeks.

Rajesh (name changed), a 52-year-old senior manager living in Powai, watched his friends panic. Colleagues were selling everything. Family WhatsApp groups were filled with "sell before it falls more" messages.
But Rajesh didn't sell a single unit.

Not because he was brave. Not because he could predict the future. But because he had a proper asset allocation strategy—one that was designed specifically for his life stage, risk capacity, and financial goals.
His portfolio: ₹82 lakh across mutual funds, PPF, and debt instruments.
During the crash, his portfolio fell by only 12%—half of what pure equity investors lost. Within 18 months, he recovered completely and hit new highs.
Here's the exact risk management framework he used. This isn't theory. This is what actually protected wealth when markets collapsed.
The Core Principle: Match Your Goal Timeline to Your Asset Type
Rajesh had three major financial goals:
1. Daughter's wedding in 2 years → Target: ₹18 lakh
2. Son's higher education in 5 years → Target: ₹25 lakh
3. His own retirement in 8 years → Target: ₹1.2 crore corpus
Here's how he allocated money for each goal:
Goal 1 (2 years away): 100% in debt (liquid funds, short-term debt funds, fixed deposits)
Why? Markets can stay down for 2-3 years. You cannot take equity risk for goals this close.
Goal 2 (5 years away): 40% equity, 60% debt
Why? Five years gives some time for equity to recover from corrections, but not enough for full equity exposure. Balanced allocation protects against timing risk.
Goal 3 (8 years away): 70% equity, 30% debt
Why? Eight years is enough for equity to ride out multiple market cycles. This allocation maximizes growth while maintaining a safety buffer.
This is called goal-based asset allocation. Each goal gets its own bucket with its own risk profile based on the timeline.
Most investors make one fatal mistake: They put all their money in equity (or all in debt) regardless of when they actually need it. That's not investing—that's gambling with your life goals.
The 3-Bucket System That Works for Mumbai Families
Rajesh used a simple 3-bucket framework that any family can implement:
Bucket 1: Emergency + Short-Term Goals (0-3 years)
Amount: ₹22 lakh
Allocation: 100% liquid/debt
Products: Liquid funds, ultra-short-term debt funds, FD in bank
Why: Money you need in 0-3 years should NEVER be in equity. Markets don't care about your daughter's admission deadline.
Bucket 2: Medium-Term Goals (3-7 years)
Amount: ₹28 lakh
Allocation: 50% equity, 50% debt
Products: Balanced advantage funds, equity index funds + debt funds
Why: Moderate timeline allows for some equity exposure, but needs debt cushion to handle volatility.
Bucket 3: Long-Term Wealth (7+ years)
Amount: ₹32 lakh
Allocation: 75% equity, 25% debt
Products: Nifty 50 index, Nifty Next 50 index, flexi-cap funds, small amount in PPF
Why: Long timeline means you can handle market cycles and benefit from equity's long-term compounding power.
This is how Rajesh's ₹82 lakh was actually structured. During the 2020 crash, Buckets 1 and 2 barely moved. Only Bucket 3 fell—but that was money he didn't need for 8+ years, so he simply held on.
The Rebalancing Rule That Locks in Gains
Every December, Rajesh reviewed his buckets. Here's what he did:
If equity in Bucket 3 grew from 75% to 85% (because of market gains), he sold some equity and bought debt to bring it back to 75:25.
If equity fell to 65%, he sold some debt and bought equity to restore 75:25.
This forced him to:
→ Sell high (when equity outperforms)
→ Buy low (when equity underperforms)
→ Maintain risk profile aligned to his goals
In 2021, when markets rallied 25%, his Bucket 3 equity grew to 82%. He rebalanced, selling ₹2.2 lakh of equity into debt funds. Three months later, markets corrected 8%—and he was protected.
Rebalancing isn't market timing. It's risk management. It locks in gains systematically without trying to predict the future.
Diversification: The Only Free Lunch in Investing
Within each bucket, Rajesh diversified further:
Equity Diversification:
→ 50% large-cap (Nifty 50 index)
→ 30% mid/small-cap (Nifty Next 50, flexi-cap funds)
→ 20% international equity (US index funds for geographic diversification)
Debt Diversification:
→ 40% liquid/ultra-short-term (for stability)
→ 30% short-term debt funds (for slightly better yield)
→ 20% PPF (for tax benefit + guaranteed return)
→ 10% bank FDs (for absolute safety)
He never put all money in one fund house, one sector, or one asset manager. Diversification protects against single-point failure.
When Franklin Templeton shut down 6 debt schemes in 2020, Rajesh had zero exposure because he was diversified across multiple fund houses. Other investors weren't so lucky.
What Happened During COVID Crash (Real Numbers)
March 23, 2020 (market bottom):
→ Bucket 1 (debt): ₹22 lakh → ₹21.8 lakh (-1%)
→ Bucket 2 (balanced): ₹28 lakh → ₹24.6 lakh (-12%)
→ Bucket 3 (equity-heavy): ₹32 lakh → ₹24 lakh (-25%)
Total portfolio: ₹82 lakh → ₹70.4 lakh (-14%)
His colleague who was 100% in equity? ₹82 lakh → ₹61.5 lakh (-25%).
December 2021 (18 months later):
→ Rajesh's portfolio: ₹1.02 crore (+24% from original ₹82 lakh)
→ Colleague's portfolio: ₹1.06 crore (+29% from original ₹82 lakh)
His colleague made slightly more. But he also had sleepless nights, panic-sold some holdings at the bottom, and took on far more risk than his age and goals justified.
Rajesh slept fine. His short-term goals were protected. His risk was managed. His wealth grew steadily.
That's the difference between gambling and investing.
Your Risk Management Checklist
Pull out your portfolio right now. Ask yourself:
→ Do I have goals with timelines? Or just random investments?
→ Is money I need in 2 years sitting in volatile equity funds?
→ Is my long-term money (8+ years) sitting in 6% FDs when it could compound at 12%+ in equity?
→ Do I rebalance annually? Or do I let winners run and losers bleed?
→ Am I diversified across fund houses, asset classes, and geographies?
If you answered 'no' or 'I don't know' to any of these, your risk management needs work.
How to Build Your Own 3-Bucket System
Step 1: List all your financial goals with timelines (marriage, education, home, retirement, etc.)
Step 2: Assign each goal to a bucket based on timeline:
→ 0-3 years: Bucket 1 (100% debt/liquid)
→ 3-7 years: Bucket 2 (50-50 equity-debt)
→ 7+ years: Bucket 3 (70-75% equity, 25-30% debt)
Step 3: Calculate how much money each goal needs. Invest that amount in the appropriate bucket.
Step 4: Set a calendar reminder for December every year. Rebalance each bucket back to target allocation.
Step 5: As goals approach (e.g., Bucket 3 goal is now 5 years away), shift it to Bucket 2 allocation.
This framework works for ₹5 lakh portfolios and ₹5 crore portfolios. It works in bull markets and bear markets. It works because it matches risk to reality.

title: Behavioral Checklist: The ₹12 Lakh Mistake a Thane Investor Made in 10 Minutes
summary: How emotional decisions destroy wealth—and the simple checklist that prevents them.
author: BM Wealth Editorial Team
content: By BM Wealth Editorial Team
February 2, 2025 | 8-Minute Read | Investment Education
The call came at 10:17 AM on a Monday:
"Sir, I sold everything. Markets were falling. I couldn't take it anymore."
Vikram (name changed), a 44-year-old marketing professional from Thane, had just panic-sold his entire equity portfolio—₹28 lakh invested over 6 years—during a 12% market correction.
He sold at the bottom. Markets recovered 18% over the next 4 months. His decision cost him approximately ₹12 lakh in opportunity loss.
This wasn't a case of bad funds or high costs. This was pure behavioral mistake—emotional decision-making destroying years of disciplined wealth building in 10 minutes.

After reviewing hundreds of investor portfolios, we've identified the same behavioral patterns repeating across Mumbai families. Here's the checklist that could have saved Vikram ₹12 lakh—and can protect your wealth from similar mistakes.
Rule 1: Decide Your Actions in Advance (Before Emotions Take Over)
Vikram's mistake happened because he had no plan for market corrections.
When markets fell 12%, he panicked. WhatsApp groups were screaming "sell before it gets worse." News channels showed red charts. He reacted emotionally—and paid a heavy price.
What he should have done: Created an action plan BEFORE the correction.
Here's what a proper behavioral checklist looks like:
If markets fall 10%: → Do nothing. Review asset allocation. Stay invested.
If markets fall 20%: → Rebalance. Sell some debt, buy equity at lower prices.
If markets fall 30%: → Increase SIP by 20-30% to buy more units at discounted NAV.
If markets fall 40%+: → Deploy emergency dry powder (pre-decided lump sum kept for such crashes).
Notice what's NOT on this list? "Panic and sell everything."
When you decide actions in advance—when you're calm, rational, and not watching red screens—you make better decisions. When crisis hits, you execute the plan. No emotion. No guesswork.

Priya, a 38-year-old architect from Bandra, followed this exact framework during March 2020. Markets fell 25%. She didn't panic. She followed her pre-written plan: rebalanced her portfolio, added ₹2 lakh from her debt bucket into equity. Today, that decision is worth ₹3.8 lakh (90% gain in 4 years).
Your Action: Write down right now—what will you do if markets fall 20% tomorrow? Have a written plan. Stick to it.
Rule 2: Separate Speculation from Core Portfolio (Different Money, Different Rules)
Ajay, a 29-year-old banker from Kandivali, made a smart decision most investors don't:
He divided his investments into two separate accounts:
1. Core Portfolio (₹18 lakh): Long-term SIPs in index funds for retirement and child's education. This money follows strict rules—no speculation, no stock tips, no crypto experiments.
2. Play Money (₹2 lakh): For trying stock tips from friends, occasional crypto bets, sector-specific punts. This is money he can afford to lose entirely without impacting his life goals.
The psychological benefit? When his ₹50,000 crypto bet went to ₹12,000, he didn't panic. It was play money—expected to be volatile. His core portfolio was safe, growing steadily at 12-14% CAGR.

But when his friend Rohan mixed everything together—putting ₹15 lakh of retirement money into "hot stock tips"—he couldn't sleep when markets fell. Eventually sold at a loss. Couldn't distinguish between long-term investing and short-term speculation.
Your Action: Open two separate investment accounts. Label one "Core/Long-Term". Label the other "Experimental/Play Money". Never mix the two. Different goals, different rules.
Rule 3: Review Performance vs. Benchmark Annually, Not Weekly
Sanjay, a 51-year-old doctor from Mulund, was checking his portfolio value every single day.
Some days it was up ₹40,000. He felt great. Some days it was down ₹35,000. He felt terrible. His emotional state was tied to daily NAV movements.
After 2 years of this stress, he sold everything and moved to fixed deposits at 6.5%—giving up on equity entirely.
The irony? His portfolio had delivered 13.2% CAGR over those 2 years—beating the Nifty 50 benchmark. But daily volatility made him feel like he was losing money.
What works better: Annual performance review against a benchmark.
Here's what Meera, a 45-year-old teacher from Ghatkopar, does instead:
She checks her portfolio twice a year—June 30 and December 31.
She compares:
→ Her portfolio return vs. Nifty 50 return (for equity portion)
→ Her debt fund return vs. CRISIL Short-Term Debt Index (for debt portion)
If her funds consistently underperform the benchmark for 2+ years, she considers switching. Otherwise, she stays invested.
She doesn't check daily NAVs. Doesn't react to news headlines. Doesn't panic during corrections.
Result? 14.8% CAGR over 8 years. Zero behavioral mistakes. Zero stress.
Your Action: Delete all portfolio tracking apps from your phone. Set two calendar reminders (June 30, December 31) to review performance vs. benchmark. That's it.
Rule 4: Ignore Stock Tips from Family WhatsApp Groups
Every Mumbai investor has experienced this:
Uncle in the family WhatsApp group: "Buy XYZ stock immediately! It will double in 6 months! My friend's cousin made ₹10 lakh!"
Rahul, a 33-year-old IT professional from Powai, fell for this trap. Put ₹5 lakh into three "hot tips" from family and friends. All three stocks fell 40-60%. ₹5 lakh became ₹2.2 lakh.
Meanwhile, his boring Nifty 50 index fund SIP—which nobody talks about in WhatsApp groups—grew steadily at 13% annually.
The hard truth: Stock tips in WhatsApp groups almost never work for retail investors. By the time the tip reaches you, smart money has already moved. You're buying at the peak.
Your Action: Have a simple rule: "No investment decisions based on WhatsApp forwards, ever." If someone gives you a stock tip, smile, nod, and ignore. Stick to your systematic plan.
Rule 5: Never Invest Money You Need in the Next 3 Years into Equity
Deepak, a 40-year-old entrepreneur from Borivali, made a classic behavioral mistake:
He had ₹22 lakh saved for his daughter's engineering admission (needed in 2 years). Instead of keeping it in debt funds or FDs, he put it in equity funds thinking "I can make extra returns."
Markets fell 15% just 6 months before he needed the money. He had to withdraw at a loss—losing ₹3.3 lakh that could have been avoided entirely.
The rule is simple: If you need money in the next 3 years, it belongs in debt/liquid funds—not equity. Markets don't care about your daughter's admission deadline.
Your Action: Map every financial goal to a timeline. 0-3 years? Debt only. 3-7 years? Balanced. 7+ years? Equity-heavy. No exceptions.
Rule 6: Avoid Recency Bias (What Happened Recently ≠ What Will Happen Next)
Recency bias is the biggest behavioral trap for investors:
When markets are up 30%, everyone feels like a genius. "I should have invested more!" "I should go 100% equity!"
When markets fall 20%, everyone feels scared. "This time is different." "Markets will never recover." "I should sell everything."
Both reactions are driven by recency bias—assuming recent trends will continue forever. They almost never do.
Suresh, a 48-year-old banker from Chembur, fought this bias with a simple rule:
"When I feel extreme confidence (markets up a lot), I rebalance toward debt."
"When I feel extreme fear (markets down a lot), I rebalance toward equity."
This forced him to sell high and buy low—opposite of what emotions told him to do.
Your Action: When you feel extreme emotion about markets (greed or fear), do the opposite of what your gut tells you. Use rebalancing to stay disciplined.
The Behavioral Checklist (Print and Keep This Near Your Desk)
Before making ANY investment decision, ask yourself:
□ Is this decision based on a written plan or an emotional reaction?
□ Am I reacting to daily market movements or following my annual review schedule?
□ Is this based on a WhatsApp tip or my own research/systematic strategy?
□ Am I mixing speculation (play money) with my core long-term portfolio?
□ Does the timeline of this goal match the asset class I'm choosing?
□ Am I experiencing recency bias (assuming recent trends will continue)?
□ Have I slept on this decision for at least 24 hours?
If you answer 'no' or 'not sure' to any of these, STOP. Don't make the decision yet. Wait 48 hours. Revisit when emotions settle.
This simple checklist could have saved Vikram ₹12 lakh. It can save you from similar mistakes.
